title: No. 47 — The Particular Structure of the New Government and the Distribution of Power Among Its Different Parts. (Madison)
paragraphs: We have reviewed the general form of the proposed government and the general mass of power allotted to it. Now I turn to the particular structure of this government and to the way that mass of power is divided among its constituent parts.

One of the main objections pressed by the more respectable opponents of the Constitution is that it supposedly violates the political maxim that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct. In building the federal government, they say, no heed seems to have been given to this essential precaution in favor of liberty. The separate departments of power are, they say, distributed and blended in a way that at once destroys all symmetry and beauty of form, and exposes some of the essential parts of the edifice to being crushed by the disproportionate weight of the others.

No political truth is certainly of greater intrinsic value, or bears the stamp of more enlightened champions of liberty, than the one on which this objection rests. When all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, are accumulated in the same hands, whether of one, of a few, or of many, and whether those hands are hereditary, self-appointed, or elected, we may justly call it the very definition of tyranny. If the federal Constitution were truly guilty of accumulating power in this way, or of mixing powers in a manner that dangerously tended toward such accumulation, no further argument would be needed to make everyone condemn the system. I am confident, however, that everyone will see that the charge cannot be supported, and that the maxim it relies on has been totally misunderstood and misapplied. To form correct ideas on this important subject, we should begin by investigating in what sense liberty requires the three great departments of power to be separate and distinct.

The oracle always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu. If he did not originate this invaluable precept of political science, he deserves at least the credit of having displayed it and urged it on mankind's attention more effectively than anyone else. Let us first try to establish what he meant on this point.

The British Constitution was to Montesquieu what Homer has been to the writers who teach the art of epic poetry. Those writers have taken the work of the immortal bard as the perfect model from which to draw the principles and rules of the epic art and by which to judge all similar works. In the same way, this great political critic appears to have treated the Constitution of England as the standard, or, in his own phrase, the mirror of political liberty, and to have set down the characteristic principles of that particular system as though they were elementary truths. To be sure we do not mistake his meaning, then, let us go back to the source from which the maxim was drawn.

The slightest look at the British Constitution shows that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments are by no means totally separate and distinct from each other. The chief executive is an integral part of the legislative authority. He alone has the prerogative of making treaties with foreign sovereigns, and these, once made, have under certain limits the force of legislative acts. He appoints every member of the judiciary department and can remove them on the address of the two Houses of Parliament, and when he chooses to consult them they form one of his constitutional councils. One branch of the legislative department likewise forms a great constitutional council to the executive head. On the other hand, it alone holds judicial power in cases of impeachment, and it has the supreme appellate jurisdiction in all other cases. The judges, for their part, are connected with the legislative department closely enough that they often attend and take part in its deliberations, though they are not admitted to a legislative vote.

The reasons on which Montesquieu bases his maxim show his meaning still further. "When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body," says he, "there can be no liberty, because apprehensions may arise lest THE SAME monarch or senate should ENACT tyrannical laws to EXECUTE them in a tyrannical manner." Again: "Were the power of judging joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control, for THE JUDGE would then be THE LEGISLATOR. Were it joined to the executive power, THE JUDGE might behave with all the violence of AN OPPRESSOR." Other passages explain some of these reasons more fully. Brief as they are here, they are enough to establish the meaning we have given to this celebrated maxim of this celebrated author.

Look at the constitutions of the individual States. The axiom has been laid down emphatically and, in some of them, in unqualified terms. Yet in not one State have the individual departments of power been kept absolutely separate and distinct. New Hampshire, whose constitution was the most recently formed, seems to have recognized fully that avoiding any mixture of these departments whatever is both impossible and unwise. She has qualified the doctrine by declaring "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT; OR AS IS CONSISTENT WITH THAT CHAIN OF CONNECTION THAT BINDS THE WHOLE FABRIC OF THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE INDISSOLUBLE BOND OF UNITY AND AMITY." Her constitution accordingly mixes the departments in several ways. The Senate, a branch of the legislative department, also sits as a judicial court to try impeachments. The President, who heads the executive department, also presides over the Senate, where he has an equal vote in all cases and a casting vote in a tie. The executive head is himself elected each year, in the final stage, by the legislative department, and his council is chosen each year by that department from among its own members. Several officers of state are also appointed by the legislature. And the members of the judiciary department are appointed by the executive department.

The constitution of Massachusetts has been sufficiently cautious, though less pointed, in stating this fundamental article of liberty. It declares "that the legislative department shall never exercise the executive and judicial powers, or either of them; the executive shall never exercise the legislative and judicial powers, or either of them; the judicial shall never exercise the legislative and executive powers, or either of them." This declaration corresponds exactly to Montesquieu's doctrine as we have explained it, and the plan of the Convention violates it at no point. It goes no further than to forbid any one of the entire departments from exercising the powers of another. Yet the very Constitution that carries this declaration admits a partial mixture of powers. The chief executive has a qualified negative on the legislative body. The Senate, which is part of the legislature, is a court of impeachment for members of both the executive and the judiciary departments. The members of the judiciary department can be appointed by the executive department, and removed by the same authority on the address of the two legislative branches. Finally, the legislative department appoints a number of the officers of government each year. Appointment to office, executive office in particular, is by its nature an executive function. So on this last point at least, the framers of that Constitution violated the rule they themselves set.

I pass over the constitutions of Rhode Island and Connecticut, because they were formed before the Revolution, and even before the principle we are examining had become a subject of political attention.

The constitution of New York contains no declaration on this subject, but it plainly appears to have been framed with an eye to the danger of improperly blending the different departments. It nevertheless gives the chief executive a partial control over the legislative department. More than that, it gives the judiciary department a like control, and it even blends the executive and judiciary departments in exercising it. In its council of appointment, members of the legislative department join the executive authority in appointing officers, executive and judiciary alike. And its court for the trial of impeachments and the correction of errors is to consist of one branch of the legislature and the principal members of the judiciary department.

The constitution of New Jersey blends the different powers of government more than any of those I have mentioned. The governor, the chief executive, is appointed by the legislature. He is chancellor and ordinary, or surrogate, of the State; he is a member of the Supreme Court of Appeals; and he presides, with a casting vote, over one of the legislative branches. That legislative branch also serves as the governor's executive council, and with him forms the Court of Appeals. The legislative department appoints the members of the judiciary department, and one branch of it can remove them on the impeachment of the other.

Under the constitution of Pennsylvania, the president, who heads the executive department, is elected each year by a vote in which the legislative department predominates. Together with an executive council, he appoints the members of the judiciary department, and he forms a court of impeachment to try all officers, judiciary as well as executive. The judges of the Supreme Court and the justices of the peace also appear to be removable by the legislature, and the executive power of pardon in certain cases appears to be referred to the same department. The members of the executive council are made EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace throughout the State.

In Delaware, the legislative department elects the chief executive each year. The speakers of the two legislative branches are vice-presidents in the executive department. The executive head, together with six others, three appointed by each of the legislative branches, forms the Supreme Court of Appeals, and he joins the legislative department in appointing the other judges. Throughout the States it appears that members of the legislature may at the same time serve as justices of the peace. In this State the members of one legislative branch are EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace, and so are the members of the executive council. The legislative department appoints the principal officers of the executive department, and one branch of it forms a court of impeachments. The legislature may remove any officer on its address.

Maryland has adopted the maxim in the most unqualified terms, declaring that the legislative, executive, and judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other. Yet her constitution lets the legislative department appoint the chief executive, and the executive department appoint the members of the judiciary.

Virginia's language on this subject is more pointed still. Her constitution declares, "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct; so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other; nor shall any person exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time, except that the justices of county courts shall be eligible to either House of Assembly." Yet we find more than this express exception for members of the inferior courts. The legislature also appoints the chief executive, together with his executive council. Two members of that council are displaced every three years at the legislature's pleasure. And the same department fills all the principal offices, executive and judiciary alike. The executive prerogative of pardon, too, is in one case vested in the legislative department.

The constitution of North Carolina declares "that the legislative, executive, and supreme judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other." At the same time, it assigns to the legislative department the appointment not only of the executive head but of all the principal officers within both the executive and the judiciary departments.

In South Carolina, the constitution makes the executive office elective by the legislative department. It also gives the legislative department the appointment of the members of the judiciary department, including even justices of the peace and sheriffs, and the appointment of officers in the executive department, down to captains in the army and navy of the State.

Georgia's constitution declares "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct, so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other." Yet we find that appointments by the legislature are to fill the executive department, and that the same authority is to exercise the executive prerogative of pardon in the end. Even justices of the peace are to be appointed by the legislature.

In citing these cases, where the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments have not been kept totally separate and distinct, I do not want to be taken as an advocate for the particular organizations of the individual State governments. I know well that, along with the many excellent principles they embody, they bear strong marks of the haste in which they were framed, and still stronger marks of the inexperience. It is all too plain that in some cases the fundamental principle under consideration has been violated by too great a mixture, and even an actual consolidation, of the different powers. And in no case has adequate provision been made for maintaining in practice the separation drawn on paper. What I have wished to show is that the charge against the proposed Constitution, that it violates the sacred maxim of free government, is warranted neither by the real meaning its author gave to the maxim nor by the sense in which it has so far been understood in America. This interesting subject will be resumed in the next paper.
